topics.title: The Universe and Our Solar System

objectives.text: identify the components of the universe
explain how bodies stay in orbit
describe the solar system
discuss how earth is affected by other bodies
discuss human's exploration of the universe
examine the effects of air masses in the Caribbean
examine the weather patterns in the Caribbean
examine the effects of tides
explain the causes of the different types of volcanic eruptions
discuss the properties of water
distinguish between hard and soft water
explain the uses of water
describe the various methods used locally for fishing
evaluate the effects of water pollution on aquatic life
investigate methods of purifying water
determine the conditions for flotation
explain importance of navigational devices used at sea
identify water safety devices
discuss the effects of diving on the human body
investigate the principles of forces
describe gravity as a force
determine the centre of gravity
investigate equilibrium
examine the principle of momentum conservation
explain the functions of simple machines
relate the structure of the skeleton to its functions
explain how the skeletal muscles function in the movement of the limb
examine the efficiency of simple machines
relate the physical properties of metals and non-metals to their uses
compare the reactivity of metals
discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using cooking or canning utensils made of aluminium
discuss the benefits of using alloys to make household items
examine the conditions which cause rusting
discuss the methods used to reduce or prevent tarnishing of metals
discuss the uses of common household chemicals
examine the properties of acids, bases and salts
differentiate among the properties of the states of matter
examine the properties of mixtures
determine appropriate separation techniques
explain the effects of cleaning agents on household appliances
distinguish between soapy (soap) and soapless detergents
discuss the effects of air pollution
justify the importance of community hygiene to the environment
discuss the use of plastics

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: The galaxy in which our solar system is found is called the
paper01.explanation: Our solar system is in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: A star is a

options.A: large ball of hot gas that gives out its own light
options.C: small rocky body in the asteroid belt

paper01.explanation: Stars, such as the Sun, produce their own light and heat by nuclear fusion.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: Small rocky bodies which orbit the sun, mostly between Mars and Jupiter, are called
paper01.explanation: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: A meteorite is

options.A: a piece of rock from space that reaches the earth's surface
options.B: a streak of light seen when a rock burns up in the atmosphere
options.C: a ball of ice and dust with a tail

paper01.explanation: A meteoroid that survives its fall and lands on earth is a meteorite; the streak of light is a meteor.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: A comet is made mainly of
paper01.explanation: Comets are icy bodies; near the sun the ice vaporises to form a glowing tail.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: The tail of a comet always points away from the sun because

options.A: radiation and solar wind from the sun push the dust and gas away
options.B: the comet is moving away from the sun
options.C: the tail is attracted by Jupiter

paper01.explanation: Solar wind and radiation pressure push the tail away from the sun.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: Pluto is now classified as a
paper01.explanation: In 2006 Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: The universe is made up of

options.B: billions of galaxies, each containing billions of stars

paper01.explanation: The Milky Way is one of many galaxies.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: A meteor ('shooting star') is

options.D: a streak of light made by a rock burning up in the atmosphere

paper01.explanation: Friction with the air heats the meteoroid until it glows.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: The nearest star to the earth is
paper01.explanation: The Sun is a medium-sized star about 150 million km away.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: Which of the following lists is in order of INCREASING size?
paper01.explanation: Planets orbit stars; galaxies contain billions of stars; the universe contains all galaxies.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: The Milky Way is best described as a
paper01.explanation: It is a spiral galaxy containing our solar system.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: A galaxy is

options.C: a large group of stars, gas and dust

paper01.explanation: Galaxies contain billions of stars.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: Which of the following lists is in order of INCREASING size?
paper01.explanation: Moon < Earth < Sun < galaxy.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: identify the components of the universe

paper01.stem: A light-year is a measure of
paper01.explanation: It is the distance light travels in one year.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: The force which keeps the planets in orbit around the sun is
paper01.explanation: The sun's gravitational pull provides the centripetal force for planetary orbits.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: The moon is a natural satellite of the
paper01.explanation: The moon orbits the earth.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: A geostationary satellite used for television broadcasts

options.A: orbits the earth once every 24 hours above the equator
options.B: orbits the earth once every hour
options.C: stays still in space while the earth moves

paper01.explanation: It moves round at the same rate as the earth turns, so it stays above the same place.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: If the force of gravity on an orbiting satellite suddenly disappeared, the satellite would

stimulus.lead: to the following diagram of a satellite orbiting the earth.
stimulus.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 420 290" width="420" height="290" role="img" aria-label="A satellite in orbit" font-family="'Times New Roman', Times, 'Liberation Serif', serif" font-size="13"><title>A satellite in orbit</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="420" height="290" fill="#fff"/><g fill="none" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="170" cy="150" r="60" fill="#fff" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="170" y="155" text-anchor="middle" fill="#000" stroke="none" font-size="12">Earth</text><circle cx="170" cy="150" r="120" fill="none" stroke-width="0.8" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><rect x="280" y="70" width="18" height="12" fill="#fff"/><line x1="270" y1="76" x2="280" y2="76"/><line x1="298" y1="76" x2="308" y2="76"/><line x1="289" y1="76" x2="330" y2="130"/><polygon points="330,130 323.8,126.7 328.5,123.2" fill="#000" stroke-width="1"/><text x="335" y="135" text-anchor="start" fill="#000" stroke="none" font-size="12">velocity</text><line x1="283" y1="82" x2="240" y2="110"/><polygon points="240,110 243.7,104.1 246.9,109" fill="#000" stroke-width="1"/><text x="215" y="100" text-anchor="middle" fill="#000" stroke="none" font-weight="bold">F</text></g></svg>

options.B: move off in a straight line

paper01.explanation: Without a centripetal force the satellite would move in a straight line at a tangent (Newton's first law).

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: The moon stays in orbit around the earth because

options.A: it is pushed by the sun
options.B: there is no gravity in space
options.D: the earth's gravity pulls on it

paper01.explanation: Gravity provides the centripetal force.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: An artificial satellite is

options.B: a man-made object placed in orbit

paper01.explanation: Examples include communication and weather satellites.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: Communication satellites are often placed in geostationary orbits so that

options.A: they move quickly across the sky
options.D: they stay above the same point on the earth's surface

paper01.explanation: Dishes on the ground can remain pointed at them.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: The further a planet is from the sun, the

options.A: longer it takes to complete one orbit
options.D: stronger the sun's pull on it

paper01.explanation: Outer planets travel further and more slowly.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: If the gravitational pull of the Earth on the Moon suddenly stopped, the Moon would

options.B: move off in a straight line
options.D: spin faster in the same orbit

paper01.explanation: Without a centre-seeking force, a body keeps moving in a straight line.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: A satellite stays in orbit because

options.A: its forward speed balances the pull of gravity
options.B: there is no gravity in space
options.C: it has engines running all the time

paper01.explanation: It is continually falling around the Earth.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: Planets closer to the Sun take less time to orbit because they

options.B: travel a shorter path and move faster

paper01.explanation: Mercury orbits in 88 days.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: The path of a planet around the Sun is
paper01.explanation: Orbits are slightly oval (ellipses).

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: A geostationary satellite appears to stay above the same point on Earth because it
paper01.explanation: It turns at the same rate as the Earth.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: explain how bodies stay in orbit

paper01.stem: The Moon takes about the same time to spin once on its axis as to orbit the Earth. As a result,

options.A: the same side of the Moon always faces the Earth
options.C: we see a full moon every night
options.D: the Moon causes eclipses every month

paper01.explanation: This is called synchronous rotation.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: The largest planet in the solar system is
paper01.explanation: Jupiter is the largest planet.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: The orbits of the planets around the sun are
paper01.explanation: Planets move in elliptical (slightly oval) orbits.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: How many planets are in our solar system?
paper01.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: Which of the following planets has NO moons?
paper01.explanation: Mercury and Venus have no moons.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: Which planet is closest to the sun?
paper01.explanation: Mercury is the innermost planet.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: Which planet is known as the 'Red Planet'?
paper01.explanation: Iron oxide on its surface gives Mars a red colour.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: The planet with the most visible rings is
paper01.explanation: Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: The earth is the ___ planet from the sun.
paper01.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: Which of the following is the correct order of planets starting from the sun?
paper01.explanation: The four inner rocky planets.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: Which planets are called gas giants?
paper01.explanation: Jupiter, Saturn (and Uranus, Neptune) are large planets made mostly of gas.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: Which labelled planet is the earth?
paper01.explanation: Earth is the third planet from the sun.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: describe the solar system

paper01.stem: Which planet takes the SHORTEST time to orbit the sun?
paper01.explanation: The planet closest to the sun (Mercury) has the shortest orbit.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: Day and night are caused by the

options.A: revolution of the earth around the sun
options.B: rotation of the earth on its axis
options.C: movement of the moon around the earth

paper01.explanation: The earth spins once every 24 hours; the side facing the sun has day.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: The time taken for the earth to revolve once around the sun is about
paper01.explanation: One revolution is one year, about 365¼ days.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: A solar eclipse occurs when the

options.A: moon is between the sun and the earth
options.B: earth is between the sun and the moon
options.C: sun is between the earth and the moon

paper01.explanation: The moon's shadow falls on part of the earth.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: Shadows are formed because

options.B: light is reflected by all objects
options.D: light travels in straight lines and cannot pass through opaque objects

paper01.explanation: An opaque object blocks the straight rays of light, leaving a region without light.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: The time from one full moon to the next is about
paper01.explanation: The lunar cycle is about 29.5 days.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: When it is daytime in Jamaica, it is night in parts of Asia because

options.A: only half of the earth faces the sun at any time
options.B: the sun goes around the earth
options.C: the moon blocks the sun in Asia
options.D: Asia is closer to the sun

paper01.explanation: As the earth rotates, each side faces the sun in turn.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: A lunar eclipse can only occur at
paper01.explanation: The earth must be between the sun and moon.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: A solar eclipse can only occur at
paper01.explanation: The moon must be between the sun and earth.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: The moon shines because it

options.C: reflects light from the earth only

paper01.explanation: The moon is a non-luminous body.

objective.topicTitle: The Universe and Our Solar System
objective.text: discuss how earth is affected by other bodies

paper01.stem: A shadow is darkest and sharpest when

options.A: the light source is very large
options.B: the light source is small (a point source)

paper01.explanation: A point source gives a sharp umbra with little penumbra.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: You are provided with the following apparatus and materials to plan and design an investigation to compare the hardness of three water samples: rain water, well water and tap water.

rows: rain water, well water, tap water

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable hypothesis for the investigation.

points: Well water is harder than tap water, and rain water is the softest.
OR: The harder the water, the more drops of soap solution are needed to form a lasting lather.
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for a clearly stated hypothesis; 1 mark for a testable hypothesis

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Outline a suitable procedure to test the hypothesis in (a) (i). Your response MUST be sequentially arranged.

points: Label three test tubes A, B and C.
Measure 10 cm³ of each water sample into its labelled test tube using the measuring cylinder.
Add soap solution one drop at a time, stopper and shake for 10 seconds after each drop.
Count the number of drops needed to produce a lather that lasts for 30 seconds (or measure the height of lather after a fixed number of drops).
Repeat for each sample and record the results in a table.
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for logical sequence (1 mark if there are flaws); 1 mark for instructional language (command verbs); 1 mark for a method linked to the hypothesis; 1 mark for using the apparatus/materials listed

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE variable which must be controlled in the investigation.

points: Volume of water sample
Concentration of soap solution
Size of drops/same dropper
Time of shaking

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Outline your expected results for the investigation.

points: Rain water will need the fewest drops of soap (softest) (1)
well water will need the most drops and may form scum (hardest), tap water in between (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Distinguish between temporary and permanent hardness of water.

points: Temporary hardness is caused by calcium/magnesium hydrogencarbonate and can be removed by boiling (1)
permanent hardness is caused by calcium/magnesium sulphate (or chloride) and cannot be removed by boiling (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of hard water.

points: Advantage: provides calcium for bones and teeth / pleasant taste / does not dissolve lead from pipes (1)
Disadvantage: wastes soap / forms scum / forms scale in kettles and pipes (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain how adding washing soda softens hard water.

points: Washing soda (sodium carbonate) reacts with the dissolved calcium and magnesium ions (1)
forming insoluble calcium/magnesium carbonate which settles out, so the ions can no longer react with soap (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Describe how water from a river is made safe to drink at a water treatment plant.

points: Screening removes large objects (1)
alum is added so fine particles coagulate and settle (sedimentation) (1)
the water is filtered through sand and gravel beds (1)
chlorine is added to kill microorganisms (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark each for any four stages in a logical order

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe how a tropical depression develops into a hurricane.

points: Warm, moist air over warm ocean water (above 26 °C) rises, creating an area of low pressure (1)
air rushes in and spirals around the centre, and as more water vapour condenses heat is released, strengthening the system (1)
when sustained winds exceed 63 km/h it is a tropical storm, and above 119 km/h a hurricane (1)

Loss of crops
Landslides
Loss of life
Power outages
Storm surge and coastal erosion

A - nail rusted (1)
B - no rust and C - no rust (1)
D - a lot of rust / rusted most (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why the water in test tube B was boiled and covered with a layer of oil.

points: Boiling removes dissolved air/oxygen from the water (1)
the oil layer stops air from dissolving back into the water (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the purpose of the drying agent (calcium chloride) in test tube C.

points: To absorb moisture/water vapour so the air is dry.

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Write the word equation for rusting.

points: Iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for reactants; 1 mark for product

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: A student claims that nails rust faster near the sea than inland.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable aim for an investigation to test the student's claim.

points: To find out whether iron nails rust faster in salt water than in fresh water.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Identify the manipulated and responding variables for the investigation in (b) (i).

points: Manipulated: salt in the water / type of water (salt or fresh) (1)
Responding: amount of rust formed / time for rust to appear (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why cars in coastal areas rust faster.

points: Sea spray deposits salt on the car (1)
salt dissolved in moisture speeds up the rusting reaction/ acts as an electrolyte (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain how galvanising protects an iron roof from rusting.

points: The iron is coated with a layer of zinc (1)
which acts as a barrier keeping air and water away from the iron (1)
zinc is more reactive, so even if scratched it corrodes instead of the iron (sacrificial protection) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO other methods of preventing rusting.

points: Painting
Oiling/greasing
Electroplating
Covering with plastic
Using desiccants/proper dry storage
Using alloys such as stainless steel

Neutral: table salt solution (1)

items.prompt: Explain why a person suffering from indigestion could take baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate).

points: Indigestion is caused by excess stomach acid (1)
baking soda is a base/alkali which neutralises the acid (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the name of the process in (a) (ii) and the general word equation for it.

points: Neutralisation (1)
Acid + base → salt + water (1)

items.prompt: Distinguish between soapy and soapless detergents in terms of how they are made and how they behave in hard water.

points: Soap is made from animal fats/vegetable oils and an alkali, while soapless detergents are made from petroleum products (1)
soap forms scum in hard water, while soapless detergents do not (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Suggest ONE environmental problem caused by non-biodegradable detergents.

points: They are not broken down by bacteria, so foam builds up in rivers (1), reducing oxygen and harming aquatic life / phosphates cause eutrophication (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

Suitable scale
Straight line of best fit through origin

points: Density = mass ÷ volume = 60 ÷ 100 (1)

points: It will float (1)

points: Partly fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume (1)
gently lower the stone on a thread into the water until fully immersed and record the new volume (1)
the difference between the two readings is the volume of the stone (1)

items.prompt: Explain why the egg floats in Y but sinks in X.

points: The salt solution is denser than fresh water (1)

in Y the upthrust equals the weight of the egg so it floats; in X the upthrust is less than its weight (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State Archimedes' principle.

points: When an object is wholly or partly immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust (1)
equal to the weight of fluid displaced (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why ships have Plimsoll lines painted on their hulls.

points: They show the maximum safe loading depth (1)
which varies with water density (fresh/salt) and season, preventing overloading and sinking (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

points: Life jacket/life raft/inflatable tube - keeps a person afloat

points: The triceps (Q) contracts while the biceps (P) relaxes (1)
pulling on the forearm bones so the arm straightens at the elbow (hinge joint); the muscles work as an antagonistic pair (1)

items.prompt: Calculate the velocity of the truck and car immediately after the collision.

points: Total momentum after = 30 000 kg m/s = (3 000 + 1 000) × v (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for correct substitution/working; 1 mark for correct answer with unit

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why double-decker buses carry passengers upstairs but luggage below.

points: Heavy loads placed low keep the centre of gravity low (1)
so the bus is more stable and less likely to topple when turning (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

points: When a car stops suddenly, passengers continue to move forward because of inertia (Newton's first law) (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the states of matter X, Y and Z.

points: X - solid
Y - liquid
Z - gas

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Compare the particles in a solid and a gas in terms of their movement and the forces of attraction between them.

points: Solid particles only vibrate about fixed positions while gas particles move quickly and randomly in all directions (1)
forces of attraction are strong in a solid and very weak in a gas (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the change of state in EACH of the following: water vapour forming droplets on a cold glass; moth balls getting smaller in a cupboard.

points: Condensation (1)
Sublimation (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State what is meant by 'plasma' and give ONE example.

points: Plasma is the fourth state of matter - a very hot, ionised gas containing charged particles (1)
e.g. lightning, the sun/stars, neon lights, plasma TV (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why sweat evaporating from the skin has a cooling effect.

points: The particles with the most energy escape from the surface of the liquid (1)
taking latent heat from the skin, so the skin cools (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Fishermen in a coastal village report a large number of dead fish after heavy rains washed fertiliser from nearby farms into the bay.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the process that results when fertilisers enter a body of water.

points: Eutrophication

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how fertilisers washed into the bay lead to the death of fish.

points: Nitrates/phosphates cause rapid growth of algae (algal bloom) (1)
the algae block light so plants below die, and the algae themselves die (1)
bacteria decompose the dead plants and algae (1)
the bacteria use up the dissolved oxygen, so the fish suffocate (1)
markScheme.guidance: 4 marks for a full explanation; 3 satisfactory; 2 partial; 1 limited

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State TWO other sources of water pollution.

points: Oil spills
Sewage
Pesticides
Industrial waste
Plastics/garbage
Sediment from erosion

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Describe ONE method of fishing used locally and state ONE disadvantage of it.

points: e.g. Trawling - a large net is dragged behind a boat (1); it damages the sea bed and catches unwanted species/young fish (1)
Long-lining - a long line with many baited hooks (1); may catch turtles, sharks and birds as bycatch (1)
Fish pots - wire traps with a funnel entrance (1); lost pots continue to trap fish (ghost fishing) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for description; 1 mark for disadvantage

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how sonar helps fishermen.

points: Sonar sends out pulses of sound which reflect off the sea bed or shoals of fish (1)
the time taken for the echo to return shows the depth/position of the fish (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why a scuba diver who returns to the surface too quickly may suffer from 'the bends'.

points: At depth the high pressure causes more nitrogen to dissolve in the blood (1)
if the diver rises quickly the pressure falls rapidly (1)
the nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles in the blood and joints, causing pain (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE way in which decompression sickness is treated.

points: Placing the diver in a decompression (hyperbaric) chamber.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Samantha was given a mixture of sand, salt and water.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Outline the steps Samantha should use to obtain dry salt and dry sand from the mixture.

points: Stir the mixture to make sure all the salt dissolves (1)
Filter the mixture - the sand remains on the filter paper as residue (1)
Wash and dry the sand (1)
Evaporate the filtrate (salt solution) to dryness/crystallise to obtain the salt (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark each for any four steps in a logical order

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Draw a labelled diagram of the apparatus used for filtration.

points: Funnel with filter paper drawn correctly (1)
Beaker/flask to collect the filtrate (1)
Labels: filter paper, residue, filtrate, funnel (any three) (1)
Clean lines, drawn with a ruler, appropriate title (1)

parts.context: Figure 11 shows a chromatogram of three food colourings, X, Y and Z.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Which food colouring contains the MOST dyes?

points: X or Z (two dyes each) - accept either

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why the start line must be drawn in pencil and not ink.

points: Ink contains dyes which would dissolve in the solvent and separate (1)
which would mix with/confuse the results; pencil (graphite) does not dissolve (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE everyday example of chromatography in the home.

points: Colours bleeding/running from clothes in the laundry.

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: A student wants to find out which solvent is BEST for removing ballpoint ink stains from cotton cloth. She has water, methylated spirit, acetone and vinegar.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable hypothesis.

points: Methylated spirit (an organic solvent) will remove ballpoint ink stains better than water, acetone or vinegar.
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for a clearly stated hypothesis; 1 mark for a testable hypothesis

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO variables which should be kept constant.

points: Size/age of the ink stain
Type of cloth
Volume of solvent
Time of soaking/rubbing

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE safety precaution when using acetone.

points: Keep away from flames (flammable)
Use in a well-ventilated area
Wear gloves/goggles

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Distinguish between a solution and a suspension.

points: In a solution the solute particles are dissolved and too small to be seen; in a suspension the particles are large and visible (1)
a solution does not settle but a suspension settles on standing (1)
a solution passes through filter paper completely, while the particles of a suspension are trapped (1)

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Community A is a farming village while Community B is next to an industrial estate with a landfill.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State ONE likely air pollutant in EACH community and its source.

points: Community A: pesticide sprays / dust from ploughing / smoke from burning crop residue (1)
Community B: sulphur dioxide/smoke from factories, methane or smoke from the landfill (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO effects of air pollution on human health.

points: Asthma
Bronchitis/respiratory infections
Lung cancer
Emphysema
Allergies
Eye irritation

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why burning plastics at the landfill is harmful.

points: Burning plastics releases toxic gases such as dioxins (1)
which cause respiratory illness and cancer and pollute the air (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Justify the importance of proper garbage collection and disposal in a community.

points: It prevents breeding of pests such as rats, flies and mosquitoes which spread disease (1)
it prevents pollution of land, surface water and groundwater (1)
it maintains the beauty of the area/tourism and prevents blocked drains and flooding (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Suggest TWO ways households can reduce the amount of waste they produce.

points: Refuse unnecessary packaging/plastic bags
Reuse containers
Recycle plastic, glass and paper
Compost kitchen waste
Repair items instead of discarding

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why stainless steel is preferred to iron for making kitchen sinks.

points: Stainless steel is an alloy containing chromium/nickel which does not rust (1)
so it stays clean, hygienic and lasts longer than iron, which would rust in the wet conditions (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of using aluminium cooking pots.

points: Advantage: light / good conductor of heat / cheap / does not rust (1)
Disadvantage: reacts with acidic foods / dents easily / may leach aluminium into food (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Complete Table 1 by calculating the upthrust on EACH object.

markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why the objects appear to weigh less in water.

points: Water exerts an upward force (upthrust) on the object (1)
which partly balances the weight, so the spring balance reads less (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State Archimedes' principle and use it to state the weight of water displaced by object D.

points: When an object is immersed in a fluid, the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced (2)
Weight of water displaced by D = 2.4 N (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for the principle; 1 mark for the value

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Predict how the reading for object A would change if it were immersed in sea water instead. Explain your answer.

points: The reading would be smaller (1)
because sea water is denser, so the same volume displaced weighs more and the upthrust is greater (1)

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: State ONE precaution to ensure accurate readings.

points: Make sure the object is fully immersed without touching the beaker
Read the spring balance at eye level
Check the balance reads zero before use
Wait until the reading is steady

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: A student wants to find out whether the density of a liquid affects how deep a floating test tube sinks.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable hypothesis.

points: The denser the liquid, the less deeply the loaded test tube will sink.
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for a clearly stated hypothesis; 1 mark for a testable hypothesis

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Outline a suitable method using a loaded test tube with a paper scale inside, and three liquids of different densities.

points: Put a paper scale inside a test tube and add sand/lead shot so it floats upright.
Fill three measuring cylinders with fresh water, salt water and methylated spirit.
Float the tube in each liquid in turn.
Read the depth to which it sinks on the scale at eye level.
Repeat and record the results in a table.
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a logical sequence (1 mark if there are flaws in the sequence); 1 mark for instructional language (command verbs); 1 mark for a method linked to the hypothesis; 1 mark for including the apparatus/materials listed

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why a ship's Plimsoll line has a separate mark for fresh water (F).

points: Fresh water is less dense than sea water (1)
so a ship must displace a larger volume of fresh water to get the same upthrust (1)
therefore it floats lower, and the fresh water mark is higher on the hull (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.context: Figure 2 shows the earth, the moon and the oceans (not to scale).

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State whether it is high tide or low tide at P and at R.

points: P - high tide (1)
R - low tide (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how the moon causes tides.

points: The moon's gravity pulls the ocean water on the side nearest to it, forming a bulge (high tide) (1)
a second bulge forms on the opposite side of the earth (1)
as the earth rotates, a place passes through two high tides and two low tides each day (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Distinguish between spring tides and neap tides.

points: Spring tides occur when the sun and moon are in line, giving very high and very low tides (1)
neap tides occur when the sun and moon are at right angles, giving the smallest tidal range (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO causes of a tsunami.

points: Underwater earthquakes
Underwater landslides
Volcanic eruptions (e.g. Kick-'em-Jenny)
Meteorite impact

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Suggest TWO actions coastal residents should take if a tsunami warning is issued.

points: Move quickly to high ground/inland
Follow evacuation routes
Stay away from the beach even if the sea draws back
Listen to official announcements

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Define the term 'tropical cyclone'.

points: A large area of low pressure over warm tropical seas (1)
with strong winds spiralling around the centre (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO ways in which buildings can be made more resistant to hurricanes.

points: Hurricane straps to secure the roof
Storm shutters on windows
Reinforced concrete walls
Building away from the coast/flood plains
Hip roofs instead of gable roofs

items.prompt: Construct a table to record the observations for EACH metal. You MUST include a suitable title.

Enclosed table with columns for metal and observation (1)
W - many bubbles, rapid reaction; X - some bubbles (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Arrange the metals in order of reactivity from MOST to LEAST reactive.

points: W, X, Z, Y

items.prompt: The metals were zinc, copper, iron and magnesium. Suggest which metal is W and which is Y.

points: W - magnesium (1)
Y - copper (1)

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Write a word equation for the reaction of zinc with hydrochloric acid.

points: Zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: Describe a test for the gas produced.

points: Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: A student suggests that the reactivity of metals can also be compared by measuring the rise in temperature of the acid.

items.prompt: State the manipulated variable, the responding variable and ONE controlled variable in this investigation.

points: Manipulated: type of metal (1)
Responding: temperature rise of the acid (1)
Controlled: volume/concentration of acid, mass/size of metal, starting temperature, time (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE safety precaution when working with dilute acid.

points: Wear safety goggles
Wear gloves
Wash spills with plenty of water
Do not heat

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why silver is used for jewellery while iron is not.

points: Silver is very unreactive (1)
so it does not corrode/rust easily and stays shiny (only tarnishes slowly) (1)
iron is more reactive and would rust in moist air (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE advantage of using aluminium rather than iron for window frames.

points: Aluminium does not rust because of its protective oxide layer (1), so the frames last longer without painting / are lighter (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for property; 1 mark for linked benefit

points: the earth is between the sun and the moon, so its shadow can fall on the moon (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain how day and night occur.

points: The earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours (1)
the side facing the sun has day while the side facing away has night (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO uses of artificial satellites.

points: Communication (TV, phone)
Weather forecasting/tracking hurricanes
GPS navigation
Observing space (telescopes)
Mapping/monitoring the earth

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why a geostationary satellite appears to stay in the same place in the sky.

points: It orbits above the equator in the same direction as the earth rotates (1)
taking exactly 24 hours for one orbit, so it keeps pace with the earth's surface (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE difference between a comet and an asteroid.

points: A comet is made of ice and dust and forms a tail near the sun (1); an asteroid is a rocky/metallic body mostly between Mars and Jupiter (1)

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Students measured the boiling point of water containing different masses of salt dissolved in 100 cm³ of water. The results are shown in Table 2.

table.title: TABLE 2: BOILING POINT OF SALT SOLUTIONS

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of boiling point against mass of salt and draw the line of best fit.

points: All six points plotted
Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale (y-axis need not start at 0)
Straight line of best fit
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Use your graph to estimate the boiling point of water containing 12 g of salt.

points: About 102.1-102.2 °C (from candidate's graph)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the relationship between the mass of salt dissolved and the boiling point.

points: The boiling point increases steadily (a straight-line relationship) as more salt is dissolved.

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Describe how the students should measure the boiling point accurately.

points: Heat the solution in a beaker until it boils steadily (1)
place the thermometer bulb in the liquid, not touching the bottom of the beaker (1)
read the thermometer at eye level when the reading stops rising (1)

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: State ONE safety precaution for this experiment.

points: Wear goggles
Use tongs/heat-proof gloves
Keep the beaker stable on a tripod and gauze
Tie back hair

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO chemical or physical differences between sea water and fresh water.

points: Sea water contains more dissolved salts
Sea water is denser
Sea water boils at a higher temperature
Sea water freezes at a lower temperature
Sea water conducts electricity better

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why fresh-water fish cannot survive in the sea.

points: Sea water is more concentrated than the fish's body fluids (1)
so water leaves the fish by osmosis (1)
the fish becomes dehydrated and dies (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Describe how pure water can be obtained from sea water in the laboratory.

points: Heat the sea water in a flask until it boils (1)
pass the steam through a water-cooled (Liebig) condenser (1)
collect the condensed pure water (distillate) in a beaker; the salt remains in the flask (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE disadvantage of desalination.

points: High energy use/cost
Concentrated brine waste harms marine life
Expensive equipment

topics.title: The Universe and Our Solar System

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Table 3 shows some information about the planets.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Describe the relationship between the distance of a planet from the sun and the time it takes to orbit the sun.

points: The further the planet is from the sun, the longer it takes to orbit (1)
the time increases more than in proportion to distance (e.g. Saturn is about 10 times further than Earth but takes about 30 times longer) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Identify the TWO gas giants in Table 3.

points: Jupiter and Saturn (both needed)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Suggest why Mercury is not a suitable place for humans to live.

points: It is very close to the sun, so it is extremely hot on the sunlit side (1)
it has almost no atmosphere/oxygen and extreme temperature changes (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why the orbits of the planets are described as elliptical.

points: The orbits are slightly oval-shaped rather than perfect circles.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO characteristics of outer space which astronauts must be protected from.

points: Lack of oxygen
Extreme temperatures
Harmful radiation
Vacuum/no pressure
Lack of gravity

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Distinguish between a flyby, an orbiter and a rover as methods of exploring other planets.

points: Flyby - a spacecraft passes close to the planet and takes measurements without stopping (1)
Orbiter - goes into orbit around the planet and studies it for a long time (1)
Rover - lands and moves around the surface collecting data/samples (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Give TWO benefits of the James Webb Space Telescope being placed in space rather than on earth.

points: The atmosphere does not blur or absorb the light
It can detect infrared radiation that the atmosphere blocks
It is not affected by weather or light pollution
It can see very distant/old galaxies

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why astronauts on the International Space Station feel weightless.

points: The station and astronauts are in free fall around the earth together (1)
so there is no support force pushing on them and they float (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: A test tube of molten candle wax was allowed to cool and its temperature was recorded every minute. The results are shown in Table 4.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of temperature against time.

points: All nine points plotted
Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Smooth curve with a flat section
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Use your graph to state the freezing point of the wax.

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why the temperature stayed constant between 3 and 6 minutes.

points: The wax was changing state from liquid to solid (freezing) (1)
as the particles form bonds and settle into fixed positions, energy (latent heat) is released (1)
this balances the heat lost to the surroundings, so the temperature stays the same (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: State the state(s) of the wax at 1 minute, 5 minutes and 8 minutes.

points: 1 min - liquid (1)
5 min - liquid and solid together (1)
8 min - solid (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of particles in a solid and in a liquid.

points: Solid: particles closely packed in a regular arrangement (1)
Liquid: particles close together but irregularly arranged (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO sources of error in this experiment.

points: Thermometer not read at eye level (parallax)
Thermometer not stirred/moved through the wax
Readings not taken at exactly one-minute intervals
Draughts changing the rate of cooling

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the change of state in EACH case: solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) turning to gas; water vapour forming frost on a freezer wall.

points: Sublimation (1)
Deposition (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Give ONE example of plasma.

points: Lightning / the sun / stars / neon signs / plasma TV (1) - a very hot ionised gas containing charged particles (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for example; 1 mark for description

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Equal volumes of four water samples were shaken with the same volume of soap solution. The height of lather formed is shown in Table 5.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Which sample is the hardest? Give a reason.

points: Well water (1)
it produced the least lather and formed scum (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: What type of hardness is present in the well water? Use the results to explain your answer.

points: Both temporary and permanent hardness (1)
boiling increased the lather, so some hardness (temporary) was removed (1)
but it did not lather as well as rain water, so some hardness (permanent) remained (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain how scum is formed.

points: Soap reacts with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water (1)
forming an insoluble solid (calcium stearate) which floats as scum (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why soapless detergents are used in washing machines in hard water areas.

points: Soapless detergents do not react with calcium and magnesium ions (1)
so they lather well and form no scum on clothes or in the machine (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of soap compared with soapless detergent.

points: Advantage: biodegradable / made from renewable fats and oils / less irritating (1)
Disadvantage: forms scum in hard water / does not work well in cold or acidic water (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Complete Table 6 by stating the use of EACH household chemical.

points: Bleach - disinfectant/stain remover/whitening (1)
Vinegar - cooking/pickling/removing lime scale (1)
Baking soda - raising agent in baking/antacid/cleaning (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why scouring powder should not be used to clean a non-stick frying pan.

points: The abrasive particles scratch and remove the non-stick coating.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of extension against load.

points: All seven points plotted
Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Straight line through the first five points, curving after
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe the relationship between load and extension for loads up to 4 N.

points: The extension is directly proportional to the load (1)
each 1 N increases the extension by 2.0 cm (straight line through the origin) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Suggest what happened to the spring for loads above 4 N.

points: The spring went past its elastic limit (1)
it stretched more than expected and may not return to its original length (permanently deformed) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: State TWO precautions to obtain accurate readings.

points: Read the rule at eye level
Wait for the spring to stop oscillating
Use a pointer fixed to the bottom of the spring
Keep the rule vertical and close to the spring

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Define the term 'elasticity'.

points: The ability of a material to return to its original shape and size after a stretching force is removed.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why rubber is used for the soles of sports shoes.

points: Rubber is elastic and absorbs shock (1)
and gives good grip (friction) on the ground (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE property and a suitable use for EACH of the following: steel; ceramic.

points: Steel: high tensile strength (1) - bridges, cables, reinforcing concrete (1)
Ceramic: hard, heat-resistant, insulator (1) - tiles, plates, oven dishes, electrical insulators (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for property; 1 mark for matching use

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why aluminium is used for overhead power cables even though copper is a better conductor.

points: Aluminium is much less dense (lighter) (1)
so the cables need fewer/lighter pylons and are cheaper, while still conducting well (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: A car of mass 1 000 kg travelling at 15 m/s collides with a stationary car of mass 1 500 kg. The cars lock together.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Calculate the momentum of the moving car before the collision.

markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for correct substitution/working; 1 mark for correct answer with unit

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Calculate the velocity of the two cars immediately after the collision.

markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for correct substitution/working; 1 mark for correct answer with unit

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the principle used in (a) (ii).

points: The law of conservation of momentum: total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after (if no external forces act).

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why a passenger not wearing a seat belt is thrown forward when a car stops suddenly.

points: The passenger continues moving forward at the car's original speed due to inertia (1)
because no force acts on him to stop him (Newton's first law) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why worn tyres increase the stopping distance of a car.

points: Worn tyres have less tread, so there is less friction/grip with the road (1)
so the braking force is smaller and the car takes longer to stop (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why a truck loaded high with cargo is more likely to overturn on a sharp bend.

points: A high load raises the centre of gravity (1)
when turning, the truck tilts and the line of action of its weight moves (1)
if it falls outside the wheelbase, the truck topples (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Define 'tare' as used on vehicles.

points: The mass of the vehicle when it is empty (unladen).

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain how the shape of an aircraft wing produces lift.

points: Air flows faster over the curved upper surface than under the flatter lower surface (1)
so the pressure is lower above the wing than below, producing an upward force (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline
